full_judgment:
3. The defendant Nos. 1-4 contested the suit by filing a joint written statements alleging, inter alia, that the suit land being khal category land has been under the possession of local people and the same has been recorded as khas land under SA Khatian No.1 and the same not having been fit for cultivation, the settlement No. 988(XIII)70-71 in favour of Mofizuddin in LA case was not legal and valid and the same was rightly cancelled and the land was rightly taken back in khas khatian of the government; that the plaintiff have no right, title and possession over the suit land and their kabalas being collusive, invalid and without valuable consideration, they are not entitled to get relief in the suit which is liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 7. Mr TH Khan with Mr Moinuddin, the learned Counsels appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submitted that both the Courts below committed error of law by not considering the grounds taken by the petitioners in the Courts below. He further submitted that all the PWs. in their deposition categorically stated that the suit land was under the possession of the petitioners and there was no canal or path over the suit plot. Be further submitted that Mr Mofizuddin, the lessee, not having violated any term of the registered kabuliyat as per finding in Misc. Case No. 20(XIII)1977-78 and his settlement having become permanent tenancy after 5 years became heritable as per clause 12 of the registered kabuliyat, the same could not be cancelled after 18 years on 22-2-1992 as per clause 13 but this vital aspect was not considered by the Courts below, causing failure of justice. He also submitted that the Courts below committed further illegality in not holding that there was no evidence on record that lessee Mofizuddin had more than 1.03 acres of land as shown in his application in LA Case No. 9/88(XII)-1970-71, the order of cancellation of settlement of a permanent tenancy on 22-2-1992 was illegal, invalid and without lawful authority. He again submitted that the Courts below also committed illegality in not considering the fact of possession of the suit land by the petitioners, payment of rents and taxes after mutating their names in the case holding. He also submitted that the Courts below committed illegality in holding that the suit was not maintainable being hit by law of res judicata due to pendency of the Revisional appeal before the Bhumi Appeal Board on the self-same matter. He finally submitted that the courts below failed to appreciate that the Civil Court Commissioner who made a sketch map, clearly stated that there were houses of the plaintiffs and also under construct house in the suit land and there was no pathway in it and the case land was under possession of the plaintiff. 

 9. The language of the two clauses are quite clear and self-explanatory which needs no further elucidation. Non-application of judicial mind to these important provisions of the registered lease deed by the Courts below, particularly by the Appellate Court, which is the final Court of fact, has been a grave error of law: inasmuch as after registration of the lease deed the legal status materially changed from a mere lessee to a full- fledged tenant with all the rights and incidents of a tenant as provided in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This error has vitiated the decision and plaintiffs-petitioners have been gravely prejudiced thereby and the case rightly deserves interference by this Court according to the principles and guidelines laid down by the Hon'ble Appellate Division. It hardly needs mention that in the instant case the Revenue Authority had no legal authority to cancel the registered lease after about 18 years on 22-2-1992. The plaintiffs and their vendor Mofizuddin were fully protected by the provisions of section 85 of the SAT Act. 

 10. Mr TH Khan, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-petitioners, has raised another point. He contends that the learned Judge of the Appellate Court went out of the way in deciding the appeal on the view that local people had acquired easement right over the land in suit. This view, Mr Khan very strongly contends, is absolutely based on no evidence. He points out that no such issue was framed by the trial Court and no evidence whatsoever was adduced by the defendants in order to establish easement right, nor any such point was formulated by the appellate Court either, but it abruptly arrived at the finding in the total absence of evidence on this point which has vitiated the impugned decision. In order to assess whether the submission of the learned Counsel had any merit or not, I examined the record in extenso and I have no hesitation to say that there is not an iota of evidence on record save and except a stray statement by the DW 2 that there is a halat used by local people. DW 1 Tahshildar did not say anything about easement right. Another thing that became apparent to me was that many statements made by DW 1 that clearly went in favour of the plaintiffs were not at all taken into consideration to the great prejudice of the plaintiffs petitioners. Non-consideration of important evidence on record is a fatal error. Having regard to the evidence on record, I have no hesitation to accept the contention of the learned Counsel that the finding as to acquisition of easement right by the people is based on no evidence, is of substance and I accept the same. The law relating to acquisition of easement right has been thoroughly misunderstood and misapplied and this error has attracted the power for interference with the impugned judgment. 

 11. Mr TH Khan also urged before me that the appellate Court was wrong in holding that the suit was not maintainable and that the plaintiffs ought to have prayed for further relief and should have paid ad valorem court fees. He submits that the plaintiffs were and are in possession of the land in suit and a cloud was created by the order of the ADC Revenue, Tangail passed on 22-2-1992 was sought to be set aside by the suit and no further relief was needed to be prayed for and court fee paid was sufficient. In view of what has been stated herein above and the legal position discussed and also having regard to the materials on record, I hold that Mr Khan is correct in his submission that the suit is maintainable in its present form and I hold accordingly.
